subtopicTitle: De Laval nozzle geometry — conical, bell (Rao contour), 80% bell

cards.front: What is the primary function of the diverging section in a De Laval nozzle?
cards.back: To accelerate the supersonic exhaust gases, converting thermal energy into kinetic energy and directing them axially to generate thrust.

cards.front: Describe the basic geometry of a conical rocket nozzle's diverging section.
cards.back: It consists of a straight cone with a constant divergence half-angle ($\alpha_{div}$), expanding linearly from the throat to the exit plane. This simplicity makes it easy to manufacture.

cards.front: What is the primary disadvantage of a conical nozzle regarding thrust efficiency, and how is this loss quantified?
cards.back: The primary disadvantage is divergence loss. Due to the straight-line expansion, exhaust gases have a velocity component perpendicular to the thrust axis. This loss is quantified by the divergence efficiency factor, $\lambda = \frac{1 + \cos\alpha_{div}}{2}$.

cards.front: How does the geometry of a bell nozzle differ from a conical nozzle, and what is its main advantage?
cards.back: A bell nozzle features a curved diverging section, typically starting with a high initial divergence angle near the throat and gradually curving to a smaller exit angle. Its main advantage is achieving higher thrust efficiency in a shorter length compared to a conical nozzle of equivalent expansion ratio.

cards.front: Explain the underlying principle and optimization goal of the 'Rao contour' for bell nozzles.
cards.back: The Rao contour, derived using the Method of Characteristics, designs the optimal nozzle wall shape to turn the exhaust flow efficiently and uniformly parallel to the nozzle axis at the exit. Its optimization goal is to maximize thrust for a given nozzle length or minimize length for a given thrust performance, by minimizing divergence loss.

cards.front: What does an '80% bell nozzle' signify in terms of geometry and performance trade-offs?
cards.back: An '80% bell nozzle' has a diverging section that is 80% of the length of a full-length (ideal) Rao contour bell nozzle for the same expansion ratio. It represents a trade-off: reduced nozzle length and weight (cost/packaging) at the expense of a small reduction (0.5-1%) in ideal thrust efficiency compared to a full bell.

cards.front: Compare the manufacturing complexity and typical thrust performance for conical, full bell (Rao), and 80% bell nozzles.
cards.back:
• Conical: Simplest to manufacture. Lowest performance (Thrust Coefficient $C_F \approx 0.95-0.97 \times C_{F,ideal}$).
  • Full Bell (Rao): Most complex to manufacture due to precise contouring. Highest performance ($C_F \approx 0.98-0.995 \times C_{F,ideal}$).
  • 80% Bell: Moderately complex. High performance, slightly less than full bell ($C_F \approx 0.975-0.985 \times C_{F,ideal}$), offering a good balance of performance, length, and weight.
